passages.original: rursum in conparatione gradum faciens dicit: adeo diuinis hominem conparari non posse, ut nec angelus possit. discernit praeterea corpus et carnem, quia cum omnis caro etiam corpus sit, non omne corpus est caro. unde apostolus: alia caro uolucrum, alia caro piscium, alia autem hominum. et corpora caelestia et corpora terrestria, euidenter ostendens terrenum corpus etiam carnem fore, caeleste uero non etiam carnem. ne forte hic aptari conueniat illud quod eundem Hieronymum dicere meminit: globos siderum corporatos esse spiritus arbitrantur, ut ipsa sidera siue angelorum corpora corpora utique caelestia sint, cum illi spiritus qui istis corporati sunt corporei non sint, sicut et deum dicimus incarnatum, et sicut ipsa anima humana incarnatur utique, cum administrandam suscipit carnem.
passages.english: Again, making a step in the comparison, he says: man can so little be compared with divine things that not even an angel can. He distinguishes, moreover, body and flesh, because while all flesh is also body, not every body is flesh. Hence the apostle: "one flesh of birds, another flesh of fishes, but another of men," and "both celestial bodies and terrestrial bodies," evidently showing that an earthly body is also flesh, but a heavenly one is not also flesh. Perhaps it may be fitting to apply here what he recalls the same Jerome saying: "they think that the globes of the stars are embodied spirits," so that the stars themselves, or the bodies of angels, are certainly heavenly bodies, while those spirits which are embodied in them are not bodily, just as we also say that God was incarnate, and just as the human soul itself is certainly incarnated when it takes on flesh to govern.
passages.notes: The quotations are from 1 Corinthians 15:39-40. The subject of "he recalls" (meminit) is unclear, probably the opponent whose arguments are being answered. The sentence beginning "ne forte" is taken as a tentative suggestion ("perhaps it may be fitting"). The syntax is loose.

passages.original: Idem Platon in libro, quem negl ϕυσιxής scripsit: anima, inquit, animantium omnium corporalis nonestipsaque se mouet aliorum quoque agitatrix, quae naturaliter mota sunt. in Phaedone autem sic apud eundem Platonem cum Simmia et Cebete aliisque philosophis Socrates loquitur, ut cum uideamus illic ualde consentanea nostrisque oppido coniuentia pronuntiari, quae non solum praeiudicio auctoritatis utuntur, sed uirtute rationis adminiculantur, animaduertamus praeter natiuum humanae mentis uigorem hasce uidelicet animas, quae tam remota persecutae sunt, tam .
passages.english: The same Plato, in the book which he wrote "On Nature", says: "The soul of all living things is not corporeal; it moves itself, and it is also the mover of the other things which are moved by nature." And in the Phaedo Socrates speaks with Simmias and Cebes and other philosophers, according to the same Plato, in such a way that, since we see things stated there that are very consistent with and wholly in agreement with our own [views], things which not only rest on the prior weight of authority but are supported by the force of reason, we should observe that, beyond the native vigour of the human mind, these souls in particular, which pursued things so remote, so
passages.notes: "negl ϕυσιxής" is a scanning error for Greek περὶ φυσικῆς ("On Nature"). "nonestipsaque" read as "non est ipsaque". "oppido coniuentia" taken as "wholly in agreement" (coniuentia, lit. "winking at, conniving with"; possibly for conuenientia). The passage breaks off mid-sentence; it continues in the following text ("...so closed things they approached, so hidden things they saw...").

passages.original: prout locorum ratio poposcit, et superiore libro discussimus et prolatis nunc summorum magnis auctorum testimoniis in rem sui nobis opitulante ueritate rationis quoque uiribus refellimus. Marcus varro, sui saeculi peritissimus et teste Tullio omnium sine dubitatione doctissimus, quid in musicis, quid <in arithmeticis), quid in geometricis, quid in philosophomenon libris diuina quadam disputatione contendit, nisi ut a uisibilibus ad inuisibilia, a localibus ad inlocalia, a corporeis ad incorporea miris aeternae artis modis abstrahat animum et in corpora, hoc est in aduersa sibi dilapsum sui compotem faciat?
passages.english: As the plan of the passages required, we both discussed [this] in the previous book and now, by bringing forward the weighty testimonies of the greatest authors on the matter, with truth helping us, we refute [it] by the force of reason as well. Marcus Varro, the most learned man of his age and, on Tullius' testimony, without doubt the most erudite of all: what does he strive for in his books on music, on arithmetic, on geometry, and in his books of philosophical topics, with a sort of divine argument, except to draw the mind, by the wonderful methods of eternal art, from visible things to invisible, from things in place to things without place, from bodily things to incorporeal, and, when it has slipped down into bodies, that is, into what is opposed to it, to make it master of itself?
passages.notes: "<in arithmeticis)" is an editorial supplement; the closing bracket is misprinted. "philosophomenon" is Greek for "[books] of philosophical matters". The opening clause continues a sentence from the preceding context ("that fiction of ignorance..."), so its object is understood from there. "Tullius" is Cicero.

passages.original: Aurelius Augustinus et acumine ingenii et rerum multitudine et operis mole ueluti quidam Chrysippus argumentandi uirtute aut Zenon sensuum subtilitate aut varro noster uoluminum magnitudine et qui profecto talis natura adtentione disciplinis exstiterit, ut non inmerito ab istis corporalibus nostri saeculi Epicureis aut Cynicis spiritalis sophista dissenserit, libro ad Hieronymum de origine animae sic pronuntiat: incorpoream esse animam etsi difficile tardioribus persuaderi potest, mihi tamen fateor esse persuasum, cumque id ita fore rationibus magnis atque insolubili argumentatione conuincat ac super hoc Hieronymi sententiam poscat, laudis suae tantum a Hieronymo scripta recuperat, quin haud dubie Hieronymus nihil de anima sentire dicit uerius, nihil disputare posse perfectius.
passages.english: Aurelius Augustine, in sharpness of intellect, number of subjects and mass of work like a Chrysippus in power of argument, or a Zeno in subtlety of thought, or our own Varro in the size of his volumes, and who indeed proved to be such by nature and by application to studies that, not undeservedly, as a spiritual sophist he has dissented from these bodily-minded Epicureans or Cynics of our age, declares thus in his book to Jerome on the origin of the soul: "That the soul is incorporeal, although it is hard to persuade slower minds of it, I confess that I am nevertheless persuaded." And when he proves by great reasons and irrefutable argument that this is so, and asks Jerome's opinion on this point, he receives from Jerome only writings in his praise, to the effect that Jerome says, without doubt, that nobody could think more truly about the soul, nobody could argue more perfectly.
passages.notes: The final clause ("quin haud dubie...") is awkward; it is taken as reporting Jerome's praise of Augustine. "talis natura adtentione disciplinis" is probably corrupt or compressed, perhaps "natura [et] adtentione".
